newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Few signs of Israeli slowdown abating -economists.
newsitem.headline: Few signs of Israeli slowdown abating -economists.

text.p: As the Israeli economy's slowdown marks its one-year anniversary economists see few signs of a pick-up in the near term and most say they are expecting relatively modest growth for the rest of the decade.

"All told, we have entered a period of slower growth than we enjoyed in the 1990-95 period....That rate of growth won't reappear at least until the year 2000," said Hezy Gutman, chief economist at First International Bank of Israel.

After six years of rapid expansion capped by a 7.1 percent increase in gross domestic product (GDP) in 1995, Israel's economy began slackening in the second quarter of 1996. For the full year, it grew just 4.4 percent.

In the first quarter of 1997, GDP expanded by a 2.8 percent annualised rate. That marked an improvement from a very weak final quarter in 1996, but most economists say the data do not point to a clear revival of growth.
An analysis by Bank Hapoalim of the last quarter of 1996 and first quarter of 1997 showed a mix picture.

"Against the decline in private consumption, there were increases in exports and no growth in investments in fixed assets," said Ptachia Bar-Shavit, the bank's chief economist, who estimates GDP will grow at a 2.5-3.0 percent rate the rest of the year.
"Is a recovery on the way? It's not at all clear," he said.
Economists say the conditions that created a boom in consumer spending and exports, setting off the breathless expansion in the first half of the decade, are unlikely to be repeated.

"The 1990-95 years were special. You rarely have a coming together of so many positive developments -- immigration, the peace process, the opening of new world markets and the cancellation of the Arab boycott," said Gutman.
In those years, some 600,000 immigrants mainly from the former Soviet Union poured into Israel, just as the collapse of the communist bloc opened new export markets for Israel.

In 1993, former Prime Minister Yitzhak Rabin shook hands with PLO leader Yassir Arafat on the White House lawn formally launching the peace process. That reduced the perceived political risk of doing business with Israel, sparking a wave of foreign investment.
The six-year celebration came to a halt half-way through 1996 as the central bank put on the monetary brakes and a series of bus bombings early in 1996 caused a downturn in tourism.

Economists said political risk has increased with the election of Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu last May, but they are divided whether another breakthrough in the peace process, such as an agreement with Syria, would rekindle rapid growth.
Gutman said it could, as would another surge of immigration, but Debbie Bennellick, emerging markets economist at UBS Ltd in London, is sceptical.
"Politics was not a big factor in the slowdown, why should we expect it to create such a dramatic acceleration," she said. "It's much more connected with internal factors."
The key factor is renewed export growth, economists said.

"From 1992 to 1995 there were three main engines of growth -- exports, private consumption and to a lesser extent investment," said Bar-Shavit. "Private consumption won't grow as fast in the future because until now it was influenced by immigration. As a result, exports must grow 12 percent for the economy to grow six percent."
Israel Discount Bank, in a report released this week, forecast growth of no more than three percent next year.

Gutman is a little more optimistic, predicting 3.5 percent, with the pace ranging between three and four percent through the year 2000, maybe a little higher. Bennellick is looking for a smarter 4.5 percent.
"We'll see a recovery but not growth rates of six to seven percent -- lower but sustainable rates," she said.
